title: Clothes, Colours and Buying Things
overview: Buying clothes needs more language than buying food, because you have to describe what you want before anyone can help you find it. This unit teaches where an adjective goes, the four words for pointing at things near and far, how to ask for a different size or colour once you have seen the first one, and how to say that something is not quite right. It ends with a returns notice, because the moment you most need to read one is after you have already bought the thing.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. It covers all four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is short and card 4 is the one people get backwards.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a returns notice.
Do the Practice. Practice 5 asks you to find a real one.
Record yourself asking for three different things in a shop.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Buying clothes takes more language than buying food. With food you can point. With clothes you have to say what you want before anybody can find it for you — the size, the colour, and whether the first one was right.
Four patterns.
The first is where the adjective goes, and English is strict about it. The describing word comes BEFORE the thing. A blue shirt. A warm coat. A small size.
Not a shirt blue. Many languages put it after, and this is one of the most immediately noticeable differences when you start describing things.
If you have more than one adjective, they go in a rough order — size, then colour. A small blue shirt. A long black coat. There is a longer order that English speakers follow without knowing it, and you do not need it at this level. Size then colour will carry you a long way.
And the adjective never changes. Not for plural, not for anything. A blue shirt, two blue shirts. Blue stays blue.
Second pattern: this, that, these, those. Four words, and they divide in two ways at once.
Near or far. This and these are near you. That and those are away from you.
One or more than one. This and that are one. These and those are more than one.
So: this shirt, one and near. That shirt, one and far. These shoes, more than one and near. Those shoes, more than one and far.
In a shop you will use all four constantly, because you are pointing at things at different distances. How much is this? Have you got these in blue? I like that one.
Third pattern: asking for a different one. You already know how to ask a price, from Unit 4. This is what you say after the answer.
Have you got this in a larger size? Have you got it in blue? Have you got anything cheaper?
The shape is the same each time: have you got, then it or this, then in, then what you want different. In a larger size. In blue. In something warmer.
And one more, which is the most useful sentence in the unit: Can I try it on? Notice the word on at the end. Try it means test it in general; try it on means put it on your body. In a clothes shop you want try it on, and leaving off the on will usually still be understood but it is worth getting right.
Fourth pattern: too and enough. These say that something is not right, and they are opposites in a way that catches people.
Too means more than you want. Too big. Too expensive. Too tight.
Enough means as much as you need. Big enough. Warm enough.
And here is the part that catches everybody: too goes BEFORE the adjective, and enough goes AFTER it. Too big. Big enough. Not enough big.
It is the only word in this whole level that goes after the adjective, and that is exactly why it is easy to get backwards.
One last thing. The negative of enough is the most useful form of all: not big enough, not warm enough, not long enough. That is how you say something is too small without being rude about it, and in a shop it is the sentence you will reach for most.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing for the upper body, usually with buttons.
words.example: I need a white shirt for work.
practice: I need a white shirt for work.
This shirt is too small.
Have you got this shirt in blue?
The shirt has a pocket.
These shirts are all the same size.
words.starter: I need a white shirt for
words.tutor: Describe a shirt using two adjectives in the right order — size then colour.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing covering both legs. Always plural in English.
practice: These trousers are too long.
I need a pair of black trousers.
Have you got these trousers in a smaller size?
The trousers do not fit.
Those trousers are more comfortable.
words.tutor: Trousers is always plural, so it takes these and those, never this or that. Say it both ways and hear which is wrong.

words.meaning: Things you wear on your feet.
words.example: These shoes are not big enough.
practice: These shoes are not big enough.
I need new shoes for work.
Have you got these shoes in brown?
The shoes are very comfortable.
Those shoes are too expensive.
words.tutor: Say what is wrong with a pair of shoes using not big enough, then using too small.

words.meaning: A long piece of clothing worn over your other clothes when it is cold.
practice: I need a warm coat.
This coat is not warm enough.
Have you got a longer coat?
The coat has two pockets.
That grey coat is nice.
words.tutor: Say what kind of coat you need, using two adjectives.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing worn by women, covering the body and part of the legs.
practice: That blue dress is nice.
The dress is too long.
Have you got this dress in a larger size?
She needs a dress for the interview.
These dresses are all the same price.
words.tutor: Notice dress is also a verb. Use it as a noun here.

words.meaning: A short coat.
practice: This jacket is too tight.
I need a light jacket for the summer.
Have you got this jacket in black?
The jacket has no pockets.
That jacket is not warm enough.
words.tutor: Say what is wrong with a jacket, once with too and once with not … enough.

words.meaning: The colour of night, the darkest colour.
practice: I need black trousers.
Have you got this in black?
The black one is more expensive.
She always wears black.
A black coat goes with everything.
words.tutor: Ask for something in black. Use the have you got … in shape.

words.meaning: The colour of snow, the lightest colour.
words.example: A white shirt is best for work.
practice: A white shirt is best for work.
Have you got it in white?
The white one gets dirty quickly.
I need two white shirts.
White is not practical.
words.tutor: Say why you would or would not choose white. Use because.

words.meaning: The colour of a clear sky.
words.example: Have you got this in blue?
practice: Have you got this in blue?
I prefer the blue one.
A dark blue jacket is useful.
The blue is nicer than the grey.
These come in blue and black.
words.tutor: Ask for a different colour. Then say which you prefer.

words.meaning: The colour of grass and leaves.
practice: The green one is cheaper.
I do not like green.
Have you got a green one?
The green jacket is warmer.
Green and brown go well together.
words.tutor: Compare two colours using a comparative from Unit 4.

words.meaning: The colour of earth and wood.
practice: Brown shoes go with everything.
Have you got these in brown?
The brown ones are more comfortable.
I need brown, not black.
That brown coat is very warm.
words.tutor: Say which colour you would choose and why.

words.meaning: The colour between black and white.
practice: A grey coat is practical.
Have you got it in grey?
The grey one is not warm enough.
I prefer grey to black.
These grey trousers fit well.
words.tutor: Say what you prefer, using prefer … to.

words.meaning: A place where things are sold.
practice: The shop closes at six.
This shop is more expensive.
I bought it in that shop.
The shop is next to the market.
Which shop did you go to?
words.tutor: Say when a shop opens and closes, using the times from Unit 5.

words.meaning: To be the right size for somebody.
practice: These do not fit.
Does it fit?
The jacket fits well.
They fit but they are not comfortable.
Nothing in this shop fits me.
words.tutor: Notice fit and comfortable are different. Say a sentence where something fits but is not comfortable.

words.meaning: To test something, or to put clothes on to see if they fit.
practice: Can I try it on?
Try the larger size.
I tried three and none of them fitted.
Can I try these on?
You should try it before you buy it.
words.tutor: Say try it and try it on. Ask the tutor what the difference is.

words.meaning: To take something back to the shop.
words.example: Can I return it if it does not fit?
practice: Can I return it if it does not fit?
I returned the shoes yesterday.
You cannot return sale items.
Return it within fourteen days.
She returned it without the receipt.
words.tutor: Ask whether you can return something. This is worth asking before you buy.

words.meaning: To swap something for a different one.
words.example: Can I exchange it for a larger size?
practice: Can I exchange it for a larger size?
They will exchange it but not refund it.
I exchanged it for a blue one.
You can exchange it within a month.
Exchange is easier than return.
words.tutor: Ask to exchange something. Notice the word for after exchange.

words.meaning: The place in a shop where you pay.
practice: Pay at the till.
The till is at the front of the shop.
There is a queue at the till.
Ask at the till if you are not sure.
The notice is behind the till.
words.tutor: Ask where the till is, then ask one question at it. The returns notice says to ask there.

words.meaning: Too close to the body; not loose enough.
practice: This jacket is too tight.
The shoes are a little tight.
It is tight across the shoulders.
These are tighter than the others.
Not too tight, please.
words.tutor: Say where something is tight. Being specific about the place gets you better help.

words.meaning: Not close to the body; the opposite of tight.
practice: The trousers are too loose.
I prefer a looser fit.
It is loose at the waist.
A loose shirt is cooler.
These are looser than those.
words.tutor: Say too loose and then not tight enough. Notice they mean the same thing.

words.meaning: Measuring a lot from end to end.
practice: The sleeves are too long.
I need a longer coat.
It is long enough.
The dress is not long enough.
These trousers are longer than those.
words.tutor: Say too long and not long enough about different things.

words.meaning: Not long.
practice: The jacket is too short.
I need a shorter one.
The sleeves are short enough.
It is not short enough.
A short coat is easier on the bus.
words.tutor: Say the same problem two ways: too short, and not long enough.

words.meaning: Keeping heat in; not cold.
words.example: This coat is not warm enough.
practice: This coat is not warm enough.
I need something warmer.
It is warm enough for the spring.
A warm jacket is essential here.
That one is warmer than this one.
words.tutor: Say what you need using warmer, then using not warm enough.

words.meaning: Pleasant to wear; not causing pain.
practice: These shoes are very comfortable.
It fits but it is not comfortable.
I need comfortable shoes for work.
The most comfortable ones are the cheapest.
Comfortable is more important than cheap.
words.tutor: Comfortable is a long word, so it takes more, not er. Say more comfortable and hear why.

words.meaning: To decide which one you want.
words.example: I cannot choose between these two.
practice: I cannot choose between these two.
Choose the one that fits.
She chose the blue one.
It is difficult to choose.
You should choose comfort over price.
words.tutor: Say you cannot choose between two things. Use between from Unit 2.

words.meaning: To like one thing more than another.
practice: I prefer the blue one.
She prefers black to brown.
Which do you prefer?
I prefer comfortable shoes.
I prefer this to that.
words.tutor: Say what you prefer using prefer … to. Notice it is to, not than.

words.meaning: To make a choice after thinking about it.
practice: I have not decided yet.
Decide before the shop closes.
She decided to take the larger size.
I decided against it.
It is hard to decide.
words.tutor: Say you have not decided. This is a useful thing to say in a shop.

words.meaning: A reduced price for a limited time.
words.example: There is an offer on coats this week.
practice: There is an offer on coats this week.
The offer ends on Friday.
Is this on offer?
The offer is two for the price of one.
Items on offer cannot be returned.
words.tutor: Ask whether something is on offer. Note the phrase on offer.

words.meaning: An amount taken off the usual price.
words.example: Is there a discount on this?
practice: Is there a discount on this?
They gave me a discount.
There is no discount on sale items.
The discount is only for members.
Ask about a discount before you pay.
words.tutor: Ask about a discount politely. Notice this is a question, not a demand.

readings.title: Three Sentences and You Can Buy Anything
readings.passage:
You do not need many words to buy clothes. You need three sentences, and you need them to arrive quickly.
The first says what you want. I am looking for a warm coat. That is all. Two adjectives at most, and the thing.
The second asks for a change. Have you got this in a larger size? Have you got it in blue? Have you got anything cheaper?
The third says what is wrong. It is too small. It is not warm enough. The sleeves are too long.
That is the whole conversation. Everything else is decoration.
One thing worth knowing. If you cannot remember a word for a piece of clothing, describe what it does. Something for the rain. Something warm for my legs. Something to wear under a jacket. A shop assistant will find it, and you will learn the word from the answer, which is a better way of learning it than from a list.
And say can I try it on. Not can I try it — that means test it in general. On is the word that means put it on your body, and in a clothes shop it is the one that matters.
One last piece of advice, and it has nothing to do with English. Ask about returns before you pay, not after. The answer changes what you buy.

readings.title: Sizes Do Not Agree With Each Other
readings.passage:
A size is not a measurement. It is a label, and different shops use it differently.
The same person can be one size in one shop and a different size in another, in the same week, without changing at all. This is normal, it happens to everybody, and it is not worth being upset about.
What follows from it is practical. Never buy clothes in an unfamiliar shop without trying them on, however sure you are of your size.
Sizes are usually written in one of three ways. As a word: small, medium, large. As a number: 38, 40, 42. Or as a measurement in centimetres or inches, which is the only one that means anything exact.
When you ask for a different size, you do not need the number. A larger size and a smaller size work everywhere and cannot be wrong.
Two words that are easy to confuse. Fit is about size — does it go on your body. Comfortable is about how it feels once it is on. Something can fit and not be comfortable, and if it is not comfortable in the shop it will not become comfortable later.
And one word to be careful with. When an assistant says it suits you, that is about how it looks, not about the size. It is a compliment, not information.
The useful question is always the same, and it is worth asking even when you think you know the answer: have you got this in a larger size?

readings.title: Returns and Exchanges Notice
readings.setting: The notice on the wall behind the till.
readings.passage:
RETURNS AND EXCHANGES

We will exchange or refund any item within
28 DAYS of purchase, provided that:

  · you have the original receipt
  · the item is unworn and unwashed
  · all labels are still attached

WITHOUT A RECEIPT
We can offer an exchange or a credit note only.
No cash refunds without a receipt.

SALE ITEMS
Sale items may be exchanged within 14 days.
Sale items cannot be refunded.

WE CANNOT ACCEPT RETURNS OF
  · underwear or swimwear
  · pierced jewellery
  · items altered at your request

FAULTY ITEMS
Your rights regarding faulty goods are not
affected by this notice.

Exchanges are made at the current selling price.
If the price has gone down since you bought it,
the difference will not be refunded.

Ask at the till if you are unsure.

comprehension.q: What are the three sentences the text says you need?
comprehension.a: What you want, a request for a change, and what is wrong with it.
comprehension.why: The text lists all three with an example each and says everything else is decoration.

comprehension.q: What should you do if you cannot remember the word for something?
comprehension.a: Describe what it does — something for the rain, something warm for my legs.
comprehension.why: The text adds that you then learn the word from the answer, which is better than learning it from a list because it is attached to a real need.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say to ask about returns before you pay?
comprehension.a: Because the answer changes what you buy.
comprehension.why: This is an inference the text states in one line. Knowing you cannot return something is information you need while deciding, not afterwards.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say a size is not a measurement?
comprehension.a: Because it is a label, and different shops use it differently — the same person can be different sizes in different shops.
comprehension.why: The text is explicit that this happens to everybody and is not worth being upset about, which is the point of saying it.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between fit and comfortable?
comprehension.a: Fit is about size — whether it goes on. Comfortable is about how it feels once it is on.
comprehension.why: The text adds that something can fit without being comfortable, and that if it is uncomfortable in the shop it will not improve later.

comprehension.q: An assistant says it suits you. What does the text say that means?
comprehension.a: It is about how it looks, not about the size — a compliment, not information.
comprehension.why: This is worth separating out, because a learner may take it as confirmation that the size is right when it says nothing about that.

comprehension.q: How long have you got to return something, and what three conditions apply?
comprehension.a: Twenty-eight days, provided you have the receipt, the item is unworn and unwashed, and the labels are still attached.
comprehension.why: All three conditions are bulleted together. Missing any one of them changes what the shop will do.

comprehension.q: You bought a shirt on sale twelve days ago and it does not fit. What can you do?
comprehension.a: Exchange it — sale items may be exchanged within fourteen days, but they cannot be refunded.
comprehension.why: Two rules combine: the sale-item section shortens the window to fourteen days and removes the refund. Twelve days is inside the window, so an exchange is possible but money back is not.

comprehension.q: You have lost the receipt for a full-price coat bought last week. What will the shop do?
comprehension.a: Offer an exchange or a credit note, but not a cash refund.
comprehension.why: The without-a-receipt section replaces the refund with a credit note. The twenty-eight-day window still applies, but the remedy changes.

comprehension.q: You bought a jacket for one price and it is now cheaper. You exchange it. What happens to the difference?
comprehension.a: Nothing — the notice says the difference will not be refunded.
comprehension.why: This is in the last paragraph, after the sections most people stop reading. Exchanges are made at the current selling price and the shop keeps the difference.

grammar.title: Adjective before the noun
grammar.explanation: English puts the adjective in front of the thing it describes, always. Many languages put it after, which makes this one of the most immediately noticeable differences when you start describing things.
grammar.rule:
a blue shirt        a warm coat
a small size        comfortable shoes

NOT: a shirt blue

Two adjectives — size, then colour:
  a small blue shirt
  a long black coat

The adjective never changes:
  a blue shirt · two blue shirts
grammar.workedExample:
You want a coat, it should be warm, and black.
1. Start with the thing: coat.
2. Add the adjectives IN FRONT of it, not after.
3. Two adjectives, so put them in order: size or general quality first, colour second. Warm is not a colour, so it goes first.
4. Add a at the start: a warm black coat.
Result: a warm black coat.
If you wrote a coat warm black, the meaning survives but it marks you out immediately. Move them in front.
grammar.mistake: Putting the adjective after the noun — a shirt blue. This is the direct translation from many languages and it is the single most visible beginner marker in English. It is also easy to fix, because the rule has no exceptions at this level.
grammar.tip: Describing word first, thing second. Every time.
grammar.practice:
Put the words in the right order.
1. shirt / a / white
2. coat / warm / a
3. shoes / brown / comfortable
4. jacket / a / black / short
5. trousers / grey / long
6. dress / a / blue / small
grammar.answers:
1. a white shirt  2. a warm coat  3. comfortable brown shoes  4. a short black jacket  5. long grey trousers  6. a small blue dress
In 4 and 6 the colour comes second, after the size or the general quality. That is the rough order English follows — and note that 3 and 5 take no a, because shoes and trousers are plural.

grammar.title: This, that, these, those
grammar.explanation: Four words that divide in two ways at the same time: near or far, and one or more than one. In a shop you will use all four in a single conversation, because you are pointing at things at different distances.
grammar.rule:
NEAR you    AWAY from you
  one       this        that
  more      these       those

  this shirt      that shirt
  these shoes     those shoes

Always plural in English, so always these/those:
  these trousers · these shoes
grammar.workedExample:
You are holding a pair of shoes and asking about a coat across the shop.
1. The shoes: are they near you? Yes, you are holding them. Are they one or more? Shoes is plural.
2. Near and plural: these. — How much are these?
3. The coat: near or far? Far. One or more? One.
4. Far and one: that. — Have you got that in blue?
Result: How much are these? … Have you got that in blue?
Two objects, two distances, two different words, in one conversation.
grammar.mistake: Using this with trousers or shoes. Both are always plural in English even though they are one object, so they take these and those. This trousers is wrong however single the garment is.
grammar.tip: Near or far, one or more. Two questions, one word.
grammar.practice:
Write this, that, these or those.
1. How much is ____ shirt? (in your hand)
2. How much are ____ trousers? (in your hand)
3. Have you got ____ coat in blue? (across the shop)
4. I like ____ shoes. (across the shop)
5. ____ jacket is too tight. (you are wearing it)
6. Are ____ on offer? (across the shop, several items)
grammar.answers:
1. this  2. these  3. that  4. those  5. this  6. those
Number 2 is the one to check — trousers is always plural, so it takes these even though it is one garment. Number 5 is near because you are wearing it, which is as near as anything gets.

grammar.title: Have you got this in …?
grammar.explanation: You already know how to ask a price, from Unit 4. This is what you say after the answer, and it is one frame that covers almost everything you will need in a shop.
grammar.rule:
Have you got this in a larger size?
Have you got it in blue?
Have you got anything cheaper?
Have you got anything warmer?

  have you got + this / it / anything + in + what you want

And the most useful one:
  Can I try it on?
  Can I try these on?

try it = test it     try it on = put it on your body
grammar.workedExample:
The shirt is the right style but too small. What do you say?
1. You want the same thing, different size. So the frame is have you got.
2. Point at it: this.
3. Add in.
4. Say what is different. You do not need the number — a larger size works everywhere.
Result: Have you got this in a larger size?
Then, when they bring it: Can I try it on? Note the on. Without it you have asked to test the shirt in some general way, which is not what you mean.
grammar.mistake: Leaving off the on in try it on. You will usually be understood, but try it on is the fixed phrase for clothes and it is worth having right. The other slip is asking for a specific size number in an unfamiliar shop — larger and smaller cannot be wrong, and a number can.
grammar.tip: Larger and smaller always work. A number might not.
grammar.practice:
Write what you would say.
1. The shirt is too small.
2. You want the same coat but in black.
3. Everything is too expensive.
4. You want to put the jacket on.
5. The coat is not warm enough.
6. You want to put the shoes on.
grammar.answers:
1. Have you got this in a larger size?  2. Have you got this in black?  3. Have you got anything cheaper?  4. Can I try it on?  5. Have you got anything warmer?  6. Can I try these on?
Number 6 needs these, not it, because shoes is plural — and the on stays at the end in both 4 and 6.

grammar.title: Too and enough
grammar.explanation: These both say something is not right, and they sit on opposite sides of the adjective. That is the whole difficulty, and it is worth ten minutes because you will use them constantly.
grammar.rule:
too + adjective        adjective + enough

  too big                big enough
  too expensive          warm enough
  too tight              long enough

NOT: enough big

The useful negative:
  not big enough  =  too small
  not warm enough =  too cold

enough is the only word here that goes AFTER.
grammar.workedExample:
The coat does not keep you warm. Say it two ways.
1. With too: what is there too much of? Not warmth — the problem is there is not enough. Too does not fit the positive adjective here.
2. So use the opposite adjective: it is too thin. Or too light.
3. With enough: keep the adjective you want and make it negative. It is not warm enough.
Result: It is not warm enough. (Or: it is too thin.)
Notice which one is more useful in a shop. Not warm enough tells the assistant exactly what to fix. Too thin describes the item rather than your need.
grammar.mistake: Putting enough in front — enough big. This is the only word in the whole level that follows its adjective, which is exactly why it goes wrong. If you can say big enough and warm enough automatically, the pattern is finished.
grammar.tip: Too goes before. Enough goes after. Only enough.
grammar.practice:
Write the phrase correctly.
1. The jacket is ____ (tight / too).
2. The coat is not ____ (warm / enough).
3. The trousers are ____ (long / too).
4. The sleeves are not ____ (long / enough).
5. These shoes are not ____ (big / enough).
6. This is ____ (expensive / too).
grammar.answers:
1. too tight  2. warm enough  3. too long  4. long enough  5. big enough  6. too expensive
Every odd number puts too in front; every even number puts enough after. If any of your answers read enough warm or enough long, that is the one error this card exists to remove.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Describe eight things
speaking.instructions:
Describe each of these out loud, using two adjectives in the right order.
a coat (warm, black) · a shirt (small, white) · shoes (comfortable, brown) · a jacket (short, blue) · trousers (long, grey) · a dress (small, green) · a coat (light, brown) · a shirt (large, blue)
Record all eight. Play it back and check one thing only: did every adjective come before the thing?
speaking.tutor: Describe four items to the tutor and ask it to say them back — if it changes your word order, that is the correction.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Near and far
speaking.instructions:
Look around the room you are in.
Name four things near you and four things across the room, using this, that, these and those.
At least two must be plural.
Record all eight. Play it back and check each one against two questions: was it near or far, and was it one or more?
speaking.tutor: Describe four objects to the tutor by distance and number, and ask which word each one needed.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Ask for a different one
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these out loud.
Too small → ask for larger. · Wrong colour → ask for blue. · Too expensive → ask for cheaper. · Not warm enough → ask for warmer. · You want to put it on. · You want to put the shoes on. · Too long → ask for shorter. · You cannot decide.
Record all eight. Two things to check: did every request use the same frame, and did try it on keep the on?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for six different changes and ask whether any request was unclear.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Too and enough, both ways
speaking.instructions:
For each problem, say it twice — once with too and once with not … enough.
The coat does not keep you warm. · The shirt is very tight. · The trousers cover your shoes. · The jacket ends above your waist. · The shoes hurt your feet. · It costs more than you can pay.
Twelve sentences. Record them all.
Play it back and check that enough came after the adjective every single time.
speaking.tutor: Say six problems to the tutor both ways and ask which version was clearer for a shop assistant.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — The whole purchase
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides, then change the item three times.
A: Can I help you?
B: I am looking for a warm coat.
A: What size?
B: I am not sure. Can I try this on?
A: Of course. The changing room is over there.
B: It is not warm enough. Have you got anything warmer?
A: This one is warmer, but it is more expensive.
B: How much is it?
A: Sixty.
B: Can I return it if it does not fit?
A: Within twenty-eight days, with the receipt.
B: I will take it, thank you.
Record one full version.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the assistant and buy three different items from it.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Take something back
speaking.instructions:
Without notes, play both sides of returning something.
Say what you bought and when. Say what is wrong with it, using too or not … enough. Ask whether you can exchange it or have your money back. Answer a question about whether you have the receipt. Ask what happens if you have lost it.
At least eight turns.
Record it, listen once, record it again and keep the second.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the shop and return two things — one with a receipt and one without.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Ten things, described
writing.prompt:
Write ten phrases describing clothes, each with two adjectives.
At least four must have a colour as the second adjective.
At least two must be plural, taking no a.
Underline the adjectives in each, and check they both come before the thing.
writing.model:
1. a warm black coat
2. a small white shirt
3. comfortable brown shoes
4. a short blue jacket
5. long grey trousers
6. a small green dress
7. a light brown coat
8. a large blue shirt
9. tight black trousers
10. comfortable white shoes
writing.criteria: Ten phrases; two adjectives in each; at least four with a colour second; at least two plural with no a; every adjective before the noun
writing.support: Write the ten nouns down the page first, then add adjectives in front of each. Starting from the noun makes putting the adjective after it almost impossible.
writing.extension: Turn five of them into full sentences using this, that, these or those.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Twelve problems, two ways each
writing.prompt:
Write six problems with clothes.
Write each one twice — once with too and once with not … enough.
Twelve sentences in total.
Underline too and enough in each, and check which side of the adjective they are on.
Then write one sentence saying which version you think is more useful in a shop, and why.
writing.model:
1. The coat is too thin. / The coat is not warm enough.
2. The shirt is too tight. / The shirt is not loose enough.
3. The trousers are too long. / The trousers are not short enough.
4. The jacket is too short. / The jacket is not long enough.
5. These shoes are too small. / These shoes are not big enough.
6. It is too expensive. / It is not cheap enough.
The not … enough version is more useful in a shop, because it names the thing I want more of, so the assistant knows what to bring.
writing.criteria: Six problems, each written both ways; too before the adjective and enough after it every time; the final sentence gives a real reason rather than restating the task
writing.support: Write the six too sentences first. Then for each one, ask what there is not enough of — that word becomes the adjective in the second version.
writing.extension: Write three more where too and not … enough are NOT opposites, and see whether you can find any.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Can you take it back?
writing.prompt:
Use the returns notice in Reading 3.
For each situation, write whether the shop will refund, exchange, give a credit note, or refuse — and write the reason, quoting the part of the notice that decides it.
1. A full-price shirt, eight days ago, with receipt, unworn.
2. A sale jacket, twelve days ago, with receipt, unworn.
3. A sale jacket, twenty days ago, with receipt, unworn.
4. A full-price coat, six days ago, no receipt, unworn.
5. A full-price shirt, ten days ago, with receipt, but worn once.
6. Swimwear, two days ago, with receipt, unworn.
writing.model:
1. Refund. Within 28 days, receipt, unworn, labels on — all conditions met.
2. Exchange only. Sale items may be exchanged within 14 days but cannot be refunded.
3. Refused. Sale items have only 14 days and this is 20.
4. Exchange or credit note. Without a receipt there are no cash refunds.
5. Refused. The item must be unworn.
6. Refused. Swimwear cannot be returned at all.
writing.criteria: Six answers; each names the outcome and quotes the deciding condition; number 2 and number 3 correctly distinguished by the date; number 6 identified as an absolute exclusion
writing.support: Read the notice once and write down the four things it can decide by: how long ago, receipt or not, sale or full price, and what kind of item. Then check each situation against those four.
writing.extension: Write a seventh situation of your own where two conditions conflict, and say which one wins.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I need a shirt white.
2. This trousers are too long.
3. The coat is not enough warm.
4. Can I try it?  (you mean put it on)
5. Have you got this in size larger?
6. I like that shoes.
7. It is enough big.
8. She wants a coat black long.
writing.model:
1. I need a white shirt. (Pattern 1 — the adjective comes first)
2. These trousers are too long. (Pattern 2 — trousers is always plural)
3. The coat is not warm enough. (Pattern 4 — enough goes after the adjective)
4. Can I try it on? (Pattern 3 — on is the word that means put it on your body)
5. Have you got this in a larger size? (Pattern 3 — larger comes before size)
6. I like those shoes. (Pattern 2 — shoes is plural)
7. It is big enough. (Pattern 4 — enough goes after)
8. She wants a long black coat. (Pattern 1 — both adjectives in front, size before colour)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Sort them into four piles by pattern before correcting. Two are about adjective position, two about plurals, two about enough, and two about the shop frames.
writing.extension: Numbers 3 and 7 are the same error twice. Write three more of them and check you can fix each one instantly.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Put them in order
activities.instructions:
Put the words in the right order.
1. shirt / a / white
2. coat / warm / a
3. shoes / brown / comfortable
4. jacket / a / black / short
5. trousers / grey / long
6. dress / a / blue / small
7. coat / a / light / brown
8. shirt / blue / a / large
9. shoes / white / comfortable
10. jacket / green / a / warm
11. trousers / black / tight
12. dress / a / long / white
activities.answers:
1. a white shirt  2. a warm coat  3. comfortable brown shoes  4. a short black jacket  5. long grey trousers  6. a small blue dress  7. a light brown coat  8. a large blue shirt  9. comfortable white shoes  10. a warm green jacket  11. tight black trousers  12. a long white dress
Every two-adjective phrase puts the colour second. And numbers 3, 5, 9 and 11 take no a, because shoes and trousers are plural — that is the other thing to check.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Near or far, one or more
activities.instructions:
Write this, that, these or those.
1. How much is ____ shirt? (in your hand)
2. How much are ____ trousers? (in your hand)
3. Have you got ____ coat in blue? (across the shop)
4. I like ____ shoes. (across the shop)
5. ____ jacket is too tight. (you are wearing it)
6. Are ____ on offer? (across the shop, several)
7. ____ dress is very nice. (across the shop)
8. Can I try ____ on? (shoes in your hand)
9. ____ are more comfortable. (shoes in your hand)
10. Is ____ the last one? (in your hand)
11. ____ trousers are too loose. (you are wearing them)
12. How much are ____? (several items across the shop)
activities.answers:
1. this  2. these  3. that  4. those  5. this  6. those  7. that  8. these  9. These  10. this  11. These  12. those
Every item with trousers or shoes takes these or those, whatever the distance — that is numbers 2, 4, 8, 9 and 11. If you wrote this trousers anywhere, that is the one error to fix.

activities.title: Practice 3 — What do you say?
activities.instructions:
Write what you would say in each situation.
1. The shirt is too small.
2. You want the same coat in black.
3. Everything is too expensive.
4. You want to put the jacket on.
5. The coat is not warm enough.
6. You want to put the shoes on.
7. You want to know if you can bring it back.
8. You cannot decide between two.
activities.answers:
1. Have you got this in a larger size?
2. Have you got this in black?
3. Have you got anything cheaper?
4. Can I try it on?
5. Have you got anything warmer?
6. Can I try these on?
7. Can I return it if it does not fit?
8. I cannot decide between these two.
Six of the eight use one of two frames — have you got … in, and can I try … on. That is most of what a clothes shop needs.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Too or enough
activities.instructions:
Write the phrase correctly using the words in brackets.
1. The jacket is ____ (tight, too).
2. The coat is not ____ (warm, enough).
3. The trousers are ____ (long, too).
4. The sleeves are not ____ (long, enough).
5. These shoes are not ____ (big, enough).
6. This is ____ (expensive, too).
7. The room is not ____ (warm, enough).
8. The bag is ____ (heavy, too).
9. It is not ____ (cheap, enough).
10. The shirt is ____ (loose, too).
11. It is not ____ (comfortable, enough).
12. That is ____ (short, too).
activities.answers:
1. too tight  2. warm enough  3. too long  4. long enough  5. big enough  6. too expensive  7. warm enough  8. too heavy  9. cheap enough  10. too loose  11. comfortable enough  12. too short
Every too went in front and every enough went after — six of each. If any of yours read enough warm or enough big, go back to the card. That single reversal is the only error this pattern has.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find a real returns notice
activities.instructions:
Find a real returns notice — on a wall in a shop, on the back of a receipt, or on a website.
Write down: how many days, whether a receipt is needed, what happens without one, whether sale items are different, and anything that cannot be returned at all.
Then write one sentence about what surprised you.
activities.answers:
No key — it is a real notice.
What most people find surprising: sale items usually have a shorter window and no refund; without a receipt you get a credit note rather than money; and there is nearly always a short list of things that cannot be returned at all, which is where underwear and pierced jewellery usually appear.
If your notice mentioned faulty goods separately, that is normal too — rights about faulty items are usually stronger than a shop's own policy, and a notice will often say so.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Ask before you pay
activities.instructions:
The next time you buy anything that might need to go back, ask this before you pay: can I return it if it does not fit?
Write down the answer you were given.
Then write one line about whether the answer would have changed your decision if you had heard it afterwards instead.
activities.answers:
No key.
What this is testing is not English — it is the habit. Reading 1 says the answer changes what you buy, and the only way to find out whether that is true for you is to ask before rather than after.
Most people find the answer was more restrictive than they assumed, particularly on sale items. If yours was, that is the whole lesson and it cost one sentence.

quizzes.why: English puts the adjective before the thing it describes, without exception at this level. A shirt white is the direct translation many languages produce.

quizzes.q: Which order is right for a coat that is long and black?
quizzes.why: Both adjectives go in front, and colour comes second — size or general quality first, then colour.

quizzes.q: You are holding a pair of trousers. What do you say?
quizzes.why: Trousers is always plural in English, so it takes these or those. You are holding them, so near — these.

quizzes.q: There is a coat across the shop. What do you say?
quizzes.why: One item, away from you — that. This would be right if you were holding it.

quizzes.q: The shirt is too small. What do you ask?
options: Have you got this in a larger size?
Have you got this in size larger?
Is there a size more large?
quizzes.a: Have you got this in a larger size?
quizzes.why: The frame is have you got + this + in + what you want different, and larger comes before size. Asking for larger rather than a number works in any shop.

quizzes.q: You want to put the jacket on. What do you say?
quizzes.why: Try it on is the fixed phrase for clothes. Try it means test it in some general way, and try on it puts the words in the wrong order.

quizzes.q: The coat does not keep you warm. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: Enough goes after the adjective, and the negative form is what says you need more of it. Too warm would mean the opposite problem.
Enough is the only word in this level that follows its adjective, which is exactly why it gets put in front.

quizzes.q: The notice says items may be returned within 28 days with a receipt. You have no receipt. What can the shop offer?
options: An exchange or a credit note
A refund at the sale price
quizzes.a: An exchange or a credit note
quizzes.why: The without-a-receipt section keeps the return possible but removes the cash refund. The remedy changes; the right to return does not disappear.

quizzes.q: You bought a sale jacket twenty days ago. What can you do?
quizzes.why: Sale items have a fourteen-day window, not twenty-eight, and twenty days is outside it. The shorter rule applies to sale items specifically.

quizzes.q: According to the notice, which of these can never be returned?
options: Items bought more than 28 days ago
quizzes.why: Swimwear is on the absolute exclusion list. The other three are all restricted rather than refused — a different remedy, a shorter window, or a time limit.

quizzes.q: You exchange a jacket and the price has gone down since you bought it. What happens?
quizzes.why: The last paragraph says exchanges are made at the current selling price and the difference will not be refunded. It sits after the sections most people stop reading.

teacherNotes.note: Four pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has its answer key. Practice 5 and Practice 6 are field tasks whose keys describe what the learner will probably find rather than giving a correct answer, which is the only honest way to key them.

teacherNotes.type: Adjective position is the most visible beginner marker
teacherNotes.note: A shirt blue is understood perfectly and marks a speaker immediately, which is why it survives — nothing in the conversation punishes it. It is also the easiest error in the level to fix, because the rule has no exceptions at A1. Correct it in writing, where it is visible, rather than interrupting speech.

teacherNotes.type: Enough is the only word that follows
teacherNotes.note: Every other modifier at this level goes in front, so enough big is a reasonable generalisation rather than carelessness. Say so. Learners who are told it is simply wrong keep making it; learners who are told it is the one exception tend to remember it.

Plural-only nouns catch learners on this, these and those repeatedly, and the confusion is worth naming directly: the garment is one object and the word is plural, and English is not being consistent. Practice 2 has five plural-only items out of twelve for that reason.

Four of the ten comprehension questions require combining two conditions — sale plus date, receipt plus remedy, price change plus exchange. Real notices work exactly this way, and the money is always in the interaction between two rules rather than in either one alone. Reading 1's advice to ask before paying is the practical consequence.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Learners must not be asked to give the tutor personal or financial details, and should not enter a real card number or account detail anywhere in the app. Practice 5 and 6 involve real shops; nothing collected there should be shared.

selfAssessment.statement: I can write a small blue shirt with the words in the right order.
I can point at something and say this one or that one correctly.
I can ask a shop assistant for a different size or colour.
I can say too big and not big enough without getting them backwards.
I can read a shop's returns notice and know whether I can take something back.

assignment.title: A purchase and a return
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record yourself playing both sides of buying one item of clothing, at least ten turns: say what you are looking for with two adjectives, ask to try it on, say what is wrong using both too and not … enough, ask for a different size or colour, and ask about returns before you agree to buy. Second, find a real returns notice and write the six situations from Writing 3 against it, saying what that shop would do in each case and quoting the condition that decides it. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
